title: Manaslu Circuit Trek: Full Guide
excerpt: The complete guide to the Manaslu Circuit trek: the route day by day, the Larkya La pass, acclimatization, the restricted area permit, seasons and cost.
seoTitle: Manaslu Circuit Trek: Route, Larkya La, Permit and Cost

content.value: Among the prayer flags on the Larkya La pass, at 5,106 m (16,752 ft), stands a simple wooden sign thanking trekkers for visiting Manaslu, and you reach it on day 13 of the trek, after a climb in the dark. The Manaslu Circuit trek is a circular walking journey around Manaslu, the eighth highest mountain in the world, 8,163 m, in central Nepal. It climbs along the valley of the Budhi Gandaki river, crosses the Larkya La pass and descends into the Marsyangdi valley. The area is designated a restricted area, and you enter it only with a special permit and a licensed guide. It requires no previous trekking experience, but it does require good fitness, about two weeks in Nepal and patience with the acclimatization process. The recommended seasons are spring and fall.

The Manaslu Circuit is considered one of the quietest and wildest treks in the Himalaya. In less than two weeks of walking it takes you from a narrow green river valley, among waterfalls, cliffs and suspension bridges, to Tibetan-style villages at the foot of the mountain, and from there to a high, snowy pass. This guide is based on the trek we run, the 16-day Manaslu Circuit, which also includes a day hike to Manaslu Base Camp and an acclimatization day in Samdo. It answers the questions that come up before booking: how the route is built, what the restricted area permit requires, what awaits you on the pass, what you must check before departure and what it costs.

content.value: What the Manaslu Circuit is

Manaslu rises in Gorkha district in central Nepal, close to the border with Tibet. The circuit goes around the mountain and the ridges around it: it starts at Machha Khola, at 920 m, climbs north along the Budhi Gandaki river valley to Samagaon and Samdo at the foot of the mountain, crosses the Larkya La pass and descends west to Dharapani, in the Marsyangdi river valley. At Dharapani it meets the route of the Annapurna Circuit, and from there you drive back to Kathmandu.

Along the way the landscape and the culture change. In the lower part you walk along the river, among cliffs, waterfalls, suspension bridges and bamboo forests, and pass through villages of the Gurung people. The higher you go, the more Tibetan the villages become: stone houses, monasteries, stupas, mani walls and prayer flags. Samagaon, the largest village in the area, is the cultural center of the upper valley.

Because this is a restricted area, which you enter only with a special permit and a licensed guide, far fewer trekkers come here than to the Everest and Annapurna regions. The trails are quieter, and the teahouses along the way are simpler. That is part of the charm of the trek, and part of its challenge too.
Our route, day by day
This is how the HighAir Manaslu Circuit trek is built. The altitudes in brackets are those of the overnight stop or of the high point of that day:

items: Day 1: arrival in Kathmandu and transfer to the hotel.
Day 2: preparation day in Kathmandu, a briefing with the local guides and a gear check.
Day 3: an 8 to 10 hour jeep drive from Kathmandu, along the Trishuli river, to Machha Khola (920 m).
Day 4: from Machha Khola to Jagat (1,400 m) along the Budhi Gandaki river, with a stop at the hot springs of Tatopani. Jagat is home to the entry gate of the restricted area.
Day 5: from Jagat to Deng (1,830 m), through Philim, the largest village in the area and an important checkpoint on the route.
Day 6: from Deng to Namrung (2,660 m), through forests and villages with monasteries.
Day 7: from Namrung to Lho (3,180 m), through the village of Shyala, with views of the Manaslu summit.
Day 8: from Lho to Samagaon (3,530 m), the largest and most central village in the Manaslu area.
Day 9: a day hike to Manaslu Base Camp (about 4,800 m) and back to sleep in Samagaon.
Day 10: from Samagaon to Samdo (3,860 m), past mani walls and prayer flags.
Day 11: acclimatization day in Samdo, with a walk toward the Tibetan border and back.
Day 12: from Samdo to Dharamsala (4,460 m), with rest in the afternoon.
Day 13: crossing the Larkya La pass (5,106 m) and down to Bimtang (3,590 m).
Day 14: down through rhododendron forests to Dharapani (1,860 m), the end of the circuit.
Day 15: a jeep drive via Besisahar to Kathmandu, about 9 to 10 hours, and a farewell dinner.
Day 16: transfer to the airport and flight home.

content.value: The trek has 11 days on the trail, from Machha Khola to Dharapani. Walking days last between 4 and 10 hours, and distances range from 7 to 22 km a day. The long days come early on, along the river, and on the pass day, 18 to 20 km and 8 to 10 hours of walking. The large bag, up to 15 kg per person, is carried by the porters, and you walk with a daypack only.

content.title: ✦ Five high nights before the pass
content.value: Before crossing the Larkya La you sleep five nights at 3,500 m or higher: two in Samagaon, two in Samdo and one in Dharamsala. Between them come a day hike to Manaslu Base Camp, about 4,800 m, and an acclimatization day in Samdo.
The Budhi Gandaki valley: floods and landslides

The first part of the trek runs through the Budhi Gandaki river valley, a narrow, deep valley with steep slopes. The trail crosses the river and its tributaries on suspension bridges, and in many places it runs along the mountainside, above the water. The scenery here is especially dramatic, but this is also a valley prone to floods and landslides. Heavy rain, mainly in the monsoon season and the weeks after it, can flood the river, wash away bridges and sections of trail and block the road into the valley. When that happens, the authorities may close the route until the damage is repaired.

So we will say it plainly: before any departure for the Manaslu Circuit, the condition of the trail, the bridges and the road must be checked. Check before booking and again close to departure, and set out knowing that the route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides on the ground. It is also worth checking your government's current travel advice for Nepal, and making sure your insurance covers the trek and rescue from it. We have written separately about the flood that struck the Budhi Gandaki valley and other areas of Nepal, and what it means for the trekking season.

content.value: Acclimatization: why altitude sets the pace

The main risk on the Manaslu Circuit is not technical but physiological. The higher you go, the less oxygen each breath brings in, and the body needs time to adapt. Altitude sickness usually starts with a headache, sometimes joined by loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue and nausea. When symptoms get worse despite rest at the same altitude, you descend.

On the Manaslu Circuit the walking starts low, at 920 m, and the body climbs gradually along the valley, through Jagat, Deng, Namrung and Lho, to Samagaon, 3,530 m, on day 8. On day 9 you climb to Manaslu Base Camp, about 1,270 m above Samagaon, and return to sleep in Samagaon. This is the principle of "climb high, sleep low": the body meets an altitude of about 4,800 m four days before the pass, and returns to recover lower down. In Samdo there is a full acclimatization day, and you reach Dharamsala by midday, so as to rest before the pass day.

Every group carries a pulse oximeter and a satellite device. Our rule is simple: safety before the summit. In the mountains there is no promise of reaching the goal, but there is always a commitment to safety above all.
Life in the teahouses

Throughout the trek you sleep in teahouses, the simple lodges of Nepal: bedrooms and a shared dining room. With us you sleep in twin rooms, and three meals a day, chosen from the teahouse menu, are included in the price. In a remote area like Manaslu the teahouses are more basic than in the better known regions of Nepal, especially on the higher part of the route.

What is not included are the extras the teahouses charge for separately: internet, laundry, alcohol and additional meals, so bring some cash. Anyone who prefers a single room in the teahouses can add one for 20 dollars a night.

content.value: The Larkya La pass

The Larkya La, 5,106 m, is one of the highest mountain passes in Nepal, and the highest point of the trek. You sleep before it in Dharamsala, 4,460 m, the highest overnight stop on the route, and set out in the small hours of the night, usually between 3 and 4 in the morning. This is the longest and most demanding walking day of the trek: 18 to 20 km, 8 to 10 hours of walking, 646 m of ascent and 1,516 m of descent.

The climb to the pass is long, in the cold and at high altitude, so full warm clothing, gloves and a face covering are part of the essential gear. Snow and ice are common on the pass and on the way down, and the descent to Bimtang is steep, sometimes icy, and calls for careful walking. When there is snow or ice on the trail, trekkers usually rely on microspikes and trekking poles. The weather can delay the crossing, and the decision on when to cross belongs to the guides on the ground.

From the pass a panoramic view opens over Manaslu and the peaks around it. Then you descend to Bimtang, 3,590 m, a quiet valley surrounded by peaks, and the next day continue down through rhododendron forests, which bloom in spring, to Dharapani, 1,860 m, where the circuit ends.

content.value: How hard it is, and who it suits

We grade the Manaslu Circuit as a trek of moderate difficulty. It is a trek, not a climb, and what it takes is endurance: days of 4 to 10 hours of walking with a daypack, day after day, at an altitude that rises gradually to above 4,000 m. The main difficulty is the pass day, a long day that starts in the dark, but the first two walking days, of 22 and 20 km along the river, also call for good fitness.

Previous trekking experience is not a requirement. If you can walk about 20 km a day, enjoy a challenge and come with strong motivation, the trek can suit you. The best preparation is long hikes with a pack, uphill and downhill, in the months before departure. A medical certificate and a health declaration are required from every participant, and anyone who does not meet the health or physical requirements will not be able to join.

The trek suits especially those looking for quiet, culture and wild scenery in the Himalaya, who are ready to give up some of the comfort of the busier regions in return. A full gear list is sent to every participant after registration, and before departure you receive a personal gear checklist and an online gear consultation, and the group meets the guide on an online preparation call.

Good to know: the trek is led by professional local guides from Nepal who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains. Basic English, enough to follow instructions on the trail, is worth having. Following the instructions of the crew is mandatory throughout the journey.
When to go

Nepal has two main trekking seasons: spring, before the monsoon, and fall, after it. The monsoon usually runs from June to September, and in those months the risk of floods and landslides in the Budhi Gandaki valley is at its highest. In winter, heavy snow and severe cold on the Larkya La can block the pass.

Our departures are planned for the two good windows, April and May and September and October. In spring the rhododendron forests below Bimtang are in bloom, and in the fall the skies are usually clearer. Early in the fall, close to the end of the monsoon, it is especially important to check the condition of the trail in the valley before departure. You will find the current dates on the trek page.
The restricted area permit, other permits and the visa

The Manaslu area is designated a restricted area in Nepal. To enter it you need a special permit, issued only through a trekking agency registered in Nepal, and only to those walking with a licensed guide. Independent trekking, without a guide, is not allowed. The permit is checked at the entry gate to the area at Jagat and at further checkpoints along the way. In addition to the permit you need entry permits for the conservation areas the route passes through.

From September to November the restricted area permit costs 100 US dollars per person for the first seven days and 15 dollars for each additional day, and from December to August 75 dollars and 10 dollars respectively (as of 2026). The restricted area permit and the Manaslu area entry permits are included in the price of our trek.

Most visitors, including UK, EU, US, Canadian and Australian citizens, get a Nepal tourist visa on arrival at Kathmandu airport or apply online in advance. For a 16-day trip you need the 30-day visa, which costs 50 US dollars (as of 2026) and is not included. Travel and medical insurance is not included either. Before buying, check that the policy covers trekking up to 5,106 m, including helicopter rescue, which in a remote area like this is usually the fastest way out.
Manaslu, Annapurna or Everest Base Camp

The Manaslu Circuit is close in character to the Annapurna Circuit: both are circular treks that cross one high pass, and with us both last 16 days and are graded moderate. The Larkya La is slightly lower than the Thorong La on the Annapurna Circuit, 5,416 m, but Manaslu is quieter and more remote, and entering it requires a special permit. The Everest Base Camp trek goes higher, up to Kala Patthar at 5,545 m, lasts 19 days with us and is graded hard, and at its heart is the close view of Everest, 8,848 m. We have dedicated a complete guide of its own to each of them.

content.value: What it costs and what is included

The Manaslu Circuit trek costs 2,600 US dollars per person. It includes airport transfers to the hotel in Kathmandu and back, internal transfers to the start of the route and back, 3 nights in a 5-star hotel in Kathmandu in a single room with breakfast, teahouse accommodation in shared rooms throughout the trek, dinners at a restaurant before and after the trek, three full meals a day throughout the trek, 2 liters of hot water a day, professional local English-speaking guides, porters for personal gear up to 15 kg per person, showers and toilets in the teahouses where available on the route, all entry permits for the trek, a first aid kit carried by the guides, a pulse oximeter for the group, live WhatsApp updates for families during the trek, a personal area in the HighAir app, a detailed gear list and a training plan for the trek, an online gear consultation, an online preparation call with your group and guide before departure, support with flight and travel insurance questions before departure, a gift kit with a cap, a dry-fit shirt and a 100-liter duffel bag, and a meaningful donation to the fight against cancer.

Not included: international flights, travel and medical insurance with evacuation cover (required), lunch and dinner at the hotel in Kathmandu, personal gear (clothing and footwear), tips for guides and porters (250 dollars per person), the Nepal visa (50 dollars), an extra hotel night if needed, vaccinations and travel clinic advice, and personal expenses such as drinks, alcohol, laundry, gifts and internet. At extra cost you can add a single room in the teahouses (20 dollars a night).
Note that in the event of leaving the trek early, for any reason, the additional costs, such as extra nights, meals and flight changes, are borne by the traveler.
The Manaslu Circuit with HighAir

At HighAir our Manaslu Circuit departures are planned for spring and fall. Our trek lasts 16 days, the group is limited to 10 participants, and the success rate we publish for this trek is 91 percent. When choosing a date, remember what is written here about the Budhi Gandaki valley: the condition of the trail is checked before every departure.

A portion of the proceeds from every expedition we run is dedicated to supporting cancer patients, because the mountains, in our view, are also a way of giving back. Every climber you see on the summits of the world started once, on one mountain or on one trail. If the Manaslu Circuit is your trail, we are here.
Frequently asked questions
How many days does the Manaslu Circuit trek take?

The HighAir trek lasts 16 days, from arrival in Kathmandu to departure. 11 of them are on the trail, from Machha Khola to Dharapani, including a day hike to Manaslu Base Camp and an acclimatization day in Samdo. The road from Kathmandu to the start of the trail and back is covered by jeep.
Do you need a guide and a special permit for the Manaslu Circuit?

Yes. The Manaslu area is a restricted area, and you enter it only with a special permit issued through a trekking agency registered in Nepal, and only with a licensed guide. From September to November the permit costs 100 dollars for the first seven days and 15 dollars for each additional day (as of 2026). The permit and the Manaslu area entry permits are included in the price of our trek.
How hard is the Manaslu Circuit, and do you need experience?

We grade the trek as moderate, and no previous trekking experience is required. What you need is good fitness and the ability to walk about 20 km a day, and 8 to 10 hours on the long days. The main difficulty is crossing the Larkya La pass, 5,106 m. A medical certificate and a health declaration are required from every participant.
When is the best season for the Manaslu Circuit?

Spring and fall, before and after the monsoon. Our departures are planned for April and May and for September and October. In the monsoon season, from June to September, the risk of floods and landslides in the Budhi Gandaki valley is high, and in winter heavy snow can block the pass.
Is there a risk of floods and landslides on the Manaslu Circuit?

Yes. The Budhi Gandaki valley, through which the first part of the trek runs, is prone to floods and landslides, mainly in the monsoon season and the weeks after it, and they can damage bridges and sections of trail and lead to the route being closed. That is why the condition of the trail must be checked before booking and again before departure. The route may change according to the weather and the judgment of the guides on the ground.
What language do the guides speak?
The trek is led by professional local guides from Nepal who speak English and have long experience leading groups in the mountains.
